claims.claim: Partially detached forms may represent haptomonads in the process of differentiating back into a free-swimming life cycle form.
claims.source: While it is possible that these cells became detached from the stomodeal valve during tissue fixation, these partially detached forms may also represent haptomonads in the process of differentiating back into a free-swimming life cycle form, to continue the life cycle (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed data.

claims.claim: Detachment of the cuticular lining from the epithelial cells was observed at areas of the stomodeal valve where a large number of haptomonads were adhered.
claims.source: In addition, as has been observed in previous studies (Rogers et al., 2008; Schlein et al., 1992; Volf et al., 2004), we observed a detachment of the cuticular lining from the epithelial cells at the areas of the stomodeal valve where a large number of haptomonads were adhered (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on observations from SBFSEM data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The haptomonad was attached to the stomodeal valve through the distal tip of the shortened flagellum, and the attachment interface was covered with an electron-dense attachment plaque.
claims.source: As observed in the SBFSEM data, the haptomonad was attached to the stomodeal valve through the distal tip of the shortened flagellum, and the attachment interface was covered with an electron-dense attachment plaque (Figure 2A–B).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the electron tomography data.

claims.claim: In the haptomonad cell, the asymmetric cell body extension is much shorter, with a wider anterior cell tip.
claims.source: In the haptomonad cell, this asymmetric cell body extension is much shorter, with a wider anterior cell tip (Figure 2A–C).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the electron tomography data.

claims.claim: The haptomonad flagellar pocket consisted of a bulbous region at its base and a neck region more closely apposed to the flagellum.
claims.source: The haptomonad flagellar pocket consisted of a bulbous region at its base and a neck region more closely apposed to the flagellum, with the microtubule quartet running over the bulbous region and into the neck region.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the electron tomography data.

claims.claim: In comparison with the promastigote, the neck region was shorter, and as the flagellum exited the neck region there was an expansion of the flagellum, with a large number of junctional complexes connecting the flagellar membrane to the cell body membrane.
claims.source: In comparison with the promastigote, the neck region was shorter, and as the flagellum exited the neck region there was an expansion of the flagellum, with a large number of junctional complexes connecting the flagellar membrane to the cell body membrane (Figure 2A and C).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the electron tomography data.

claims.claim: A 9+2 microtubule axoneme was present within the flagellum; however, the axoneme extended only just beyond the cell body and the central pair microtubules were not present in the final few hundred micrometres.
claims.source: A 9+2 microtubule axoneme was present within the flagellum; however, the axoneme extended only just beyond the cell body and the central pair microtubules were not present in the final few hundred micrometres (Figure 2D–F).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the electron tomography data.

claims.claim: Markham rotational averaging showed that the 9+2 axoneme was associated with accessory structures required for motility including radial spokes and inner and outer dynein arms.
claims.source: Markham rotational averaging (Gadelha et al., 2006; Skalický et al., 2017) showed that the 9+2 axoneme was associated with accessory structures required for motility including radial spokes and inner and outer dynein arms (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of electron tomography data using an established method.

claims.claim: The tip of the shortened outer doublet microtubules and central pair microtubules were capped with amorphous material and a ring-like capping structure.
claims.source: In addition, the tip of the shortened outer doublet microtubules and central pair microtubules were capped with amorphous material and a ring-like capping structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the electron tomography data.

claims.claim: In the haptomonad flagellum, the paraflagellar rod (PFR) was not observed.
claims.source: Finally, in the haptomonad flagellum, we did not observe the paraflagellar rod (PFR), an extra-axonemal structure (Figure 2D–F; Portman and Gull, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is based on observations from electron tomography data.

claims.claim: Filaments and filament bundles were present throughout the attached flagellum extending from the FAZ to the attachment interface over a distance of ~3 μm.
claims.source: Filaments and filament bundles were present throughout the attached flagellum extending from the FAZ to the attachment interface over a distance of ~3 μm (Figure 2B–C and G).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the electron tomography data.

claims.claim: These filamentous structures appeared to connect the attachment interface to the cell body via the junctional complexes.
claims.source: These filamentous structures appeared to connect the attachment interface to the cell body via the junctional complexes (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on observations from electron tomography data.

claims.claim: The attachment plaque complex consisted of several structural layers, with outer and inner dense plaques, each approximately 10 nm thick, just inside the flagellar membrane, with a dense filamentous layer (~100 nm thick) emerging from the inner dense plaque.
claims.source: The attachment plaque complex consisted of several structural layers, with outer and inner dense plaques, each approximately 10 nm thick, just inside the flagellar membrane, with a dense filamentous layer (~100 nm thick) emerging from the inner dense plaque and extending into the filamentous structures that ran towards the FAZ (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the electron tomography data.

claims.claim: The stomodeal valve had a layered structure.
claims.source: We also found that the stomodeal valve had a layered structure (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the electron tomography data.

claims.claim: A thin layer similar in appearance to the flagellar membrane, approximately 10 nm thick, was observed overlaying the cuticular layer, which is likely the wax layer composed of lipidic components.
claims.source: A thin layer similar in appearance to the flagellar membrane, approximately 10 nm thick, was observed overlaying the cuticular layer. This is likely the wax layer that is composed of lipidic components and is analogous to insect epicuticle (Figure 2G; Schmidt et al., 1998; Vincent, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is based on observations from electron tomography data with inference supported by citations.

claims.claim: No readily observable differences in the superficial and inner structure of the stomodeal valve were found between regions where haptomonads were attached, compared with the region lacking attached parasites.
claims.source: No readily observable differences in the superficial and inner structure of the stomodeal valve were found between regions where haptomonads were attached, compared with the region lacking attached parasites.
claims.evidence: This is based on observations from electron tomography data.

claims.claim: Across the majority of the attachment interface the flagellar membrane was positioned very close (~10 nm) to the stomodeal valve surface and connecting structures spanning this gap were seen.
claims.source: Across the majority of the attachment interface the flagellar membrane was positioned very close (~10 nm) to the stomodeal valve surface and connecting structures spanning this gap between the flagellar membrane and the putative wax layer of the stomodeal valve were seen (Figure 2G–H).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the electron tomography data.

claims.claim: Within the attachment interface, there were gaps where the flagellar membrane was further away from the stomodeal valve surface; these gaps corresponded to regions where connecting structures were absent.
claims.source: Within the attachment interface, there were also gaps where the flagellar membrane was further away from the stomodeal valve surface; these gaps corresponded to regions where these connecting structures were absent (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the electron tomography data.

claims.claim: The haptomonad flagellar membrane did not encase the flagellum smoothly, and there were numerous projections and indentations within the membrane.
claims.source: The haptomonad flagellar membrane did not encase the flagellum smoothly, and there were numerous projections and indentations within the membrane (Figure 2B–C).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the electron tomography data.

claims.claim: Large vesicular structures were observed throughout the flagellum.
claims.source: Furthermore, large vesicular structures were observed throughout the flagellum (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the electron tomography data.

claims.claim: Several smaller vesicles were seen near the attachment interface, and in one instance, a vesicle appeared to be fusing with or budding from the flagellar membrane.
claims.source: Intriguingly, several smaller vesicles were seen near the attachment interface, and in one instance, a vesicle appeared to be fusing with or budding from the flagellar membrane (Figure 2I).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the electron tomography data.

claims.claim: In SEM imaging of cultures 72 hr after seeding promastigote cells onto scratched plastic coverslips, large clumps of cells were observed that contained a mixture of haptomonad-like cells and promastigote cells.
claims.source: In scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging of cultures 72 hr after seeding promastigote cells onto the scratched plastic coverslips, we observed large clumps of cells that contained a mixture of haptomonad-like cells with a short flagellum attached to the substrate via an attachment plaque and promastigote cells with an unattached long flagellum, in addition to individual haptomonad-like cells with a short attached flagellum (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the SEM data.

claims.claim: In SBFSEM of in vitro haptomonad-like cells, the cell body was short and wide with a short flagellum that was attached through its tip to the substrate, with an electron-dense region at the attachment interface.
claims.source: In a reassembled and modelled volume through an attached cell clump, we observed haptomonad-like cells clearly attached to the substrate with an organisation that resembled the haptomonads in the sand fly. The cell body was short and wide with a short flagellum that was attached through its tip to the substrate, with an electron-dense region at the attachment interface (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the SBFSEM data.

claims.claim: Many more dividing (1N2F or 2N2F) cells were seen in vitro than in the sand fly.
claims.source: In addition to unattached cells within the clump, many more dividing (1N2F or 2N2F) cells were seen than in the sand fly (Figure 3—video 2; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantitative comparison of SBFSEM data from in vitro and in vivo samples.

claims.claim: Unattached cells appeared to be trapped by a filamentous extracellular matrix, which was also found between haptomonad cells in the sand fly.
claims.source: The unattached cells appeared to be trapped by a filamentous extracellular matrix, which was also found between haptomonad cells in the sand fly (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the SBFSEM data from both in vitro and in vivo samples.

claims.claim: The overall organisation of the attachment structure of the in vitro haptomonad-like cell was highly similar to that of the sand fly haptomonads.
claims.source: We used serial section electron tomography to examine the 3D ultrastructure of the in vitro haptomonad-like cells. The overall organisation of the attachment structure of the in vitro haptomonad-like cell was highly similar to that of the sand fly haptomonads.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of electron tomography data from in vitro and in vivo samples.

claims.claim: The in vitro cells had a shortened attached flagellum with a 9+2 microtubule axoneme, without the PFR, a shorter and a wider anterior cell tip, with an expanded FAZ area containing typical junctional complexes.
claims.source: The in vitro cells had a shortened attached flagellum with a 9+2 microtubule axoneme, without the PFR, a shorter and a wider anterior cell tip, with an expanded FAZ area containing typical junctional complexes (Figure 3—videos 3–4, Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the electron tomography data.

claims.claim: Filamentous structures were present across the flagellum extending from the FAZ to the attachment plaque complex in in vitro haptomonad-like cells.
claims.source: Filamentous structures were present across the flagellum extending from the FAZ to the attachment plaque complex.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the electron tomography data.

claims.claim: The attachment plaque complex had a layered structure similar to that of the haptomonads in the sand fly, although the dense filament layer appeared slightly sparser in the in vitro haptomonad-like cell.
claims.source: The attachment plaque complex had a layered structure similar to that of the haptomonads in the sand fly, although the dense filament layer that is proximal to the dense plaque (towards the cell body) appeared slightly sparser in the in vitro haptomonad-like cell (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of electron tomography data from in vitro and in vivo samples.

claims.claim: The in vitro haptomonad-like cells had a slightly longer cell body, but were similar in terms of flagellum and axoneme length and cell body width compared to sand fly haptomonads.
claims.source: In addition, we compared the morphology of in vitro haptomonad-like cells with the sand fly haptomonads by measuring flagellum and axoneme length, and cell body length and width using the SBFSEM data (Figure 3D). The in vitro haptomonad-like cells had a slightly longer cell body, but were similar in terms of flagellum and axoneme length and cell body width.
claims.evidence: This is based on quantitative comparison of SBFSEM data.

claims.claim: The in vitro forms are a good foundation on which to study the molecular cell biology of haptomonads.
claims.source: Overall, the in vitro haptomonad-like cells appeared similar in cellular organisation and ultrastructure to the sand fly haptomonads, confirming that the in vitro forms are a good foundation on which to study the molecular cell biology of haptomonads.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of in vitro and in vivo forms.

claims.claim: The adhesion process in the in vitro system took between 2 and 9 hr to complete and did not appear synchronous in the population.
claims.source: The adhesion process in our system took between 2 and 9 hr to complete and did not appear synchronous in the population.
claims.evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy observations.

claims.claim: Five distinct stages in the adhesion process were identified.
claims.source: After examining 8 videos of cells adhering (showing a total of 10 adhering cells), we identified five distinct stages in the adhesion process (Figure 4—video 1; Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of time-lapse microscopy data.

claims.claim: In the first stage of adhesion (stage 1), the cells appeared to explore the surface with their flagellum, making contact as shown by the distortion of the flagellar membrane and the release of membrane 'streamers'.
claims.source: In the first stage of adhesion (stage 1), the cells appeared to explore the surface with their flagellum, making contact as shown by the distortion of the flagellar membrane and the release of membrane 'streamers' (Figure 4—videos 1–2; Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Ellis et al., 1976; Bloodgood, 1990).
claims.evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy observations and supported by citations.

claims.claim: In stage 2, a segment of the flagellum initiated adhesion to the substrate.
claims.source: In stage 2, a segment of the flagellum initiated adhesion to the substrate.
claims.evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy observations.

claims.claim: The initial point of adhesion was not restricted to the tip of the flagellum, but could be any point along the flagellum length.
claims.source: The initial point of adhesion was not restricted to the tip of the flagellum, but could be any point along the flagellum length.
claims.evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy observations.

claims.claim: Stage 3 was characterised by cells remaining more stably fixed to a specific point on the surface, with the cell being able to move relative to this point, while the attachment region appeared to slide along the length of the flagellum.
claims.source: Stage 3 was characterised by cells remaining more stably fixed to a specific point on the surface, with the cell being able to move relative to this point, while the attachment region appeared to slide along the length of the flagellum.
claims.evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy observations.

claims.claim: In cells where the initial point of adhesion was away from the base of the flagellum, a flagellum loop often formed (in the videos examined, 7 out of 10 cells attempting to attach formed a flagellum loop).
claims.source: In cells where the initial point of adhesion was away from the base of the flagellum, a flagellum loop often formed, ensuring that the cell body was in close proximity to the point of adhesion (in the videos examined, 7 out of 10 cells attempting to attach formed a flagellum loop).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of time-lapse microscopy data.

claims.claim: In stage 4, the flagellum began to shorten, and expansion of the flagellar membrane was observed, with fusion of the membrane in the looped area of the flagellum if present.
claims.source: In stage 4, the flagellum began to shorten, and expansion of the flagellar membrane was observed, with fusion of the membrane in the looped area of the flagellum if present.
claims.evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy observations.

claims.claim: In the last stage of adhesion (stage 5), there was maturation of the attachment region, with the presence of a clear attachment plaque and the cell body rotating from lying parallel to the surface to being upright.
claims.source: Finally, in the last stage of adhesion (stage 5), there was maturation of the attachment region, with the presence of a clear attachment plaque and the cell body rotating from lying parallel to the surface to being upright.
claims.evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy observations.

claims.claim: Throughout the adhesion steps, the cell body gradually became shorter and wider.
claims.source: Throughout these steps, the cell body gradually became shorter and wider.
claims.evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy observations.

claims.claim: The adhesion process of in vitro haptomonad-like cells occurs through a defined series of steps.
claims.source: When examining cells that had been allowed to adhere to glass for 24 hr, we identified each of these stages described above by SEM (Figure 4B). This suggests that the adhesion process of in vitro haptomonad-like cells occurs through a defined series of steps.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on SEM observations confirming the stages identified by time-lapse microscopy.

claims.claim: Some attempts to attach to the surface were unsuccessful (3 out of 10 cells observed attempting to attach formed an initial adhesion but then detached and swam away before flagellum disassembly).
claims.source: In addition, we noted that some attempts to attach to the surface were unsuccessful. In the videos examined, 3 out of 10 cells observed attempting to attach to the surface formed an initial adhesion but then detached and swam away before flagellum disassembly (Figure 4—video 3; Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of time-lapse microscopy data.

claims.claim: The initial stages (1-3) of adhesion are reversible in vitro.
claims.source: This suggests that in vitro at least the initial stages (1-3) of adhesion are reversible.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on observations of cells detaching during early adhesion stages.

claims.claim: As adhesion of the in vitro haptomonad-like cells progressed, the RSP4/6 and PFR2 signals shortened in parallel with the flagellum shortening.
claims.source: In promastigote cells, RSP4/6 and PFR2 had their expected localisations along the flagellum. As adhesion of the in vitro haptomonad-like cells progressed, the RSP4/6 and PFR2 signals shortened in parallel with the flagellum shortening (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy observations of tagged proteins.

claims.claim: In the very short flagellum of mature in vitro haptomonad-like cells, only a short line of RSP4/6 signal was consistently seen, with the PFR2 signal not seen in 30% (9/30) of these cells.
claims.source: Eventually, in the very short flagellum of mature in vitro haptomonad-like cells, only a short line of RSP4/6 signal was consistently seen, with the PFR2 signal not seen in 30% (9/30) of these cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
claims.evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of fluorescence microscopy data.

claims.claim: The PFR is disassembled during in vitro haptomonad-like cell adhesion.
claims.source: suggesting that the PFR is disassembled during in vitro haptomonad-like cell adhesion.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the loss of PFR2 signal in mature attached cells.

claims.claim: After 24 hr very few metacyclics had attached in comparison to promastigotes, suggesting that in vitro metacyclics have little adhesive capacity.
claims.source: To address whether metacyclics are able to attach, in vitro purified metacyclics were allowed to attach to glass for 24 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 3). After 24 hr very few metacyclics had attached in comparison to promastigotes, suggesting that in vitro metacyclics have little adhesive capacity.
claims.evidence: This is based on quantitative comparison of adhesion between promastigotes and metacyclics.

claims.claim: The addition of 1 or 2 mM EGTA to the medium had no effect on the growth of promastigotes in suspension culture.
claims.source: The addition of 1 or 2 mM EGTA to the medium had no effect on the growth of promastigotes in suspension culture (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is based on growth curve data.

claims.claim: The presence of EGTA during adhesion resulted in a dramatic reduction in the number of attached cells after 24 hr.
claims.source: However, the presence of EGTA during adhesion resulted in a dramatic reduction in the number of attached cells after 24 hr (Figure 5B–C), with an increased effect at the higher concentration of EGTA (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of adhesion in the presence of EGTA.

claims.claim: These results contrast with those reported by Hendry, 1987, who found that T. congolense adheres to substrates in vitro even in Ca2+/Mg2+-free medium.
claims.source: These results contrast with those reported by Hendry, 1987, who found that T. congolense adheres to substrates in vitro even in Ca2+/Mg2+-free medium (medium containing 1 or 10 mM EDTA, or Ca2+/Mg2+-free PBS).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with a cited previous study.

claims.claim: There are different regulatory mechanisms for adhesion in different trypanosomatids.
claims.source: Thus, our data indicate that there are different regulatory mechanisms for adhesion in different trypanosomatids.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the contrast between the current results and previous studies on T. congolense.

claims.claim: The removal of Ca2+ from the medium did not cause cells to detach.
claims.source: To examine whether the removal of Ca2+ from cells that have already attached to the substrate disrupted their attachment, we incubated attached in vitro haptomonad-like cells (formed by differentiation for 24 hr in vitro) in the medium containing 2 mM EGTA for 30 min, and then counted the number of cells that remained attached to the glass (Figure 5D). The removal of Ca2+ from the medium did not cause cells to detach (Figure 5D)
claims.evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of cell attachment after EGTA treatment.

claims.claim: Ca2+ is not required for attachment maintenance in Leishmania in vitro, which is consistent with previous studies showing that Ca2+ is not required for attachment maintenance in other trypanosomatids.
claims.source: which was consistent with the previous studies showing that Ca2+ is not required for attachment maintenance in other trypanosomatids (Molyneux et al., 1987).
claims.evidence: This is based on the current data and supported by a citation to previous studies.

claims.claim: Ca2+ is critical for adhesion formation but not maintenance in Leishmania in vitro.
claims.source: Overall, our results suggest that Ca2+ is critical for adhesion formation but not maintenance in Leishmania in vitro.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing EGTA inhibits adhesion formation but not maintenance.

claims.claim: The structural architecture of the haptomonad attachment plaque consisted of discrete layers, with the inner and outer dense plaques overlaying the flagellar membrane connecting to a dense filament layer.
claims.source: The electron tomography observations also revealed that the structural architecture of the haptomonad attachment plaque consisted of discrete layers, with the inner and outer dense plaques overlaying the flagellar membrane connecting to a dense filament layer, summarised in Figure 6A.
claims.evidence: This is based on electron tomography observations.

claims.claim: The arrangement of the haptomonad attachment plaque is similar to that of the hemidesmosome formed in mammalian epithelial cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, this is a similar arrangement to that of the hemidesmosome formed in mammalian epithelial cells when they attach to the basement membrane (Todorović et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural similarity, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: No orthologues of the constituent proteins of the hemidesmosome are found in the L. mexicana genome.
claims.source: This has been noted before and previously the attachment plaque has been termed a hemidesmosome Killick-Kendrick et al., 1974; however, as no orthologues of the constituent proteins of the hemidesmosome are found in the L. mexicana genome, we use the term attachment plaque.
claims.evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and knowledge of protein orthology.

claims.claim: The thickness of the filaments in the haptomonad flagellum is 8–10 nm, which is similar to the thickness of intermediate filaments or septin filaments in other eukaryotes.
claims.source: The thickness of the filaments in the haptomonad flagellum is 8–10 nm, which is similar to the thickness of intermediate filaments or septin filaments in other eukaryotes (Bridges et al., 2014; Coulombe and Wong, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is based on measurements from electron microscopy data and comparison with cited literature.

claims.claim: The filament bundle in the haptomonad flagellum may be formed by bundling of individual filaments.
claims.source: In addition, the thickness of the filament bundle is 16–20 nm and just as intermediate or septin filaments can form a bundle, the filament bundle in the haptomonad flagellum may be formed by bundling of these individual filaments.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed thickness and comparison with other filament systems.

claims.claim: No orthologues of intermediate filament and septin filament proteins are present in the Leishmania genome.
claims.source: However, again, no orthologues of intermediate filament and septin filament proteins, such as keratins or septins, are present in the Leishmania genome.
claims.evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and knowledge of protein orthology.

claims.claim: Leishmania may have unique filament-forming proteins constituting the filamentous structures in the haptomonad flagellum.
claims.source: Leishmania may therefore have unique filament-forming proteins constituting the filamentous structures in the haptomonad flagellum.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the absence of known filament protein orthologues.

claims.claim: Connections observed in the gap between the surface of the stomodeal valve and the flagellar membrane are more likely to represent transmembrane protein(s), rather than flexible substances such as mucus material.
claims.source: Connections were observed in the gap between the surface of the stomodeal valve and the flagellar membrane. These connections spanned gaps with a constant spacing of ~10 nm, and were not seen in the regions where the gap was wider. This suggests that they have a specific size and are therefore more likely to represent transmembrane protein(s), rather than flexible substances such as mucus material.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the consistent spacing of the connections.

claims.claim: There has been a dramatic remodelling of the flagellum in the haptomonad.
claims.source: Overall, there has been a dramatic remodelling of the flagellum in the haptomonad.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement based on all the structural observations.

claims.claim: The strong attachment of the cell to the cuticle of the valve is not just mediated by the attachment plaque but is buttressed by the numerous filaments and filament bundles, which connect the attachment interface to the junctional complexes of the FAZ.
claims.source: The strong attachment of the cell to the cuticle of the valve is not just mediated by the attachment plaque but is buttressed by the numerous filaments and filament bundles, which connect the attachment interface to the junctional complexes of the FAZ.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed structural organization.

claims.claim: The vesicles within the flagellum may represent the mechanism by which flagellar membrane is removed and transported back to the cell body during flagellum disassembly.
claims.source: Numerous vesicles and vesicular structures were seen within the flagellum. The disassembly of the flagellum during haptomonad differentiation requires a reduction in the amount of flagellar membrane and these vesicles may represent the mechanism by which this membrane is removed and transported back to the cell body, albeit recognising the potential impediment caused by basal body and associated structures.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed vesicles.

claims.claim: The smaller vesicles near the attachment interface may contain components that are delivered for assembly of the attachment plaque.
claims.source: However, in addition to these larger vesicular structures there were smaller vesicles seen in close proximity to the attachment interface, with one in the process of fusing to or budding from the flagellar membrane at this point. The attachment plaque is a complex structure associated with a specialised membrane domain requiring many different components that need to be delivered to the attachment interface for assembly. It is entirely feasible that these components are packaged into vesicles before delivery to the interface and not without precedence as the assembly of desmosome connections between mammalian cells occurs through the delivery of vesicles loaded with desmosome proteins in a calcium dependent manner (Burdett and Sullivan, 2002).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by analogy to desmosome assembly and a citation.

claims.claim: The attachment interface could potentially support exo/endocytosis and may be important for the release of factors such as chitinase directly onto the cuticle surface of the stomodeal valve.
claims.source: Alternatively, while the flagellar pocket in Leishmania is generally thought of as the only site of exo/endocytosis, the attachment interface could potentially support these processes and may be important for the release of factors such as chitinase directly onto the cuticle surface of the stomodeal valve.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed vesicles near the attachment interface.

claims.claim: While the majority of haptomonads examined only had one flagellum and one nucleus, examples of cells dividing were seen.
claims.source: Previous work had suggested that the L. mexicana haptomonad form was non-replicative (Gossage et al., 2003) and while the majority of haptomonads we examined only had one flagellum and one nucleus, we saw examples of cells dividing.
claims.evidence: This is based on observations from SBFSEM data and contrasts with a cited previous study.

claims.claim: The dividing haptomonads could represent an asymmetric differentiation division in which one of the daughter cells differentiates to become a different life cycle stage.
claims.source: The fate of the daughter cells from these divisions has yet to be determined; however, they could represent an asymmetric differentiation division as seen in other kinetoplastids in which one of the daughter cells differentiates to become a different life cycle stage (Peacock et al., 2018; Rotureau and Van Den Abbeele, 2013; Skalický et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to similar processes in other kinetoplastids.

claims.claim: In a dividing cell with a long new flagellum both the old and new flagella were attached to the surface, suggesting that this is a proliferative division, with both daughter cells remaining attached.
claims.source: Yet, in a dividing cell with a long new flagellum both the old and new flagella were attached to the surface, suggesting that this is a proliferative division, with both daughter cells remaining attached.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of both flagella being attached.

claims.claim: In dividing cells with a short new flagellum there was no evidence of any attachment structures, suggesting that this is post-axonemal assembly modification and requires the flagellum to assemble to a length able to engage with the stomodeal valve before this process begins.
claims.source: In addition, in those dividing cells with a short new flagellum there was no evidence of any attachment structures, suggesting that this is post-axonemal assembly modification and requires the flagellum to assemble to a length able to engage with the stomodeal valve before this process begins.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of attachment structures in cells with short new flagella.

claims.claim: Sexual recombination in Leishmania has been shown to occur in the sand fly.
claims.source: Sexual recombination in Leishmania has been shown to occur in the sand fly and the close positioning of attached haptomonads may facilitate the requisite cell fusion events (Akopyants et al., 2009; Inbar et al., 2013; Peacock et al., 2011; Sadlova et al., 2011; Serafim et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claims.source: We have devised a model to summarise our current understanding of the process of Leishmania adhesion, by combining these observations from our volume electron microscopy from the sand fly derived haptomonads and light microscopy of the in vitro haptomonad-like cells, with the caveat that the in vitro processes may not perfectly replicate the sand fly situation (Figure 6B). A free-swimming promastigote cell first starts to explore the surface of the substrate using its flagellum.
claims.evidence: This is part of a model based on the combined observations from the study.

claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing calcium dependence of adhesion.

claims.claim: The initial stages of adhesion in vitro are reversible.
claims.source: Currently, we do not know whether the promastigote to haptomonad differentiation is reversible or not. In our time-lapse videos, we saw promastigotes that would adhere to the surface but would not fully adhere and instead detach and swim off. This suggests that the initial stages of adhesion in vitro at least are reversible.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on time-lapse observations of cells detaching during early adhesion.

claims.source: Around this stage, however, a point of no return occurs and the parasites from our in vitro data were unable to detach from the surface.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cells do not detach after a certain stage.

claims.source: Adhesion continues with the disassembly of the axoneme and PFR, expansion of the flagellar membrane and the assembly of the attachment plaque with the cell body reducing in length and widening.

claims.claim: The detailed 3D organisation and architecture of the haptomonad attachment revealed in this study will be of great help for future work on the identification of proteins involved in adhesion.
claims.source: The detailed 3D organisation and architecture of the haptomonad attachment and its process of adhesion development revealed in this study will be of great help for future work on the identification of proteins involved in adhesion and understanding the mechanism of the haptomonad attachment and its role in the Leishmania life cycle.
claims.evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about the implications of the study.

results.result: SBFSEM imaging of L. mexicana-infected sand flies at 10 days post-infection revealed dense haptomonad colonization of the stomodeal valve with specific morphological characteristics. Haptomonads were present in layers on both sides of the valve, with flagellum length varying by distance from the surface. Attached cells had shorter, wider cell bodies compared to unattached cells, and the majority (83%) attached via the distal flagellar tip while 17% attached laterally. The axoneme in tip-attached cells extended only just beyond the cell body, whereas in laterally attached cells it extended further along the flagellum.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C27 are well-supported by quantitative SBFSEM data with appropriate sample sizes (n=50 attached, n=39 unattached, n=17 lateral). The morphological measurements are presented with standard deviations and are directly observable in the imaging data. The spatial organization and structural details are consistently documented across multiple cells.

results.result: Cells with laterally attached flagella may represent transitional forms differentiating to or from the haptomonad stage, and most unattached cells and laterally attached cells had metacyclic/leptomonad morphology.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C29 involve speculative interpretations of morphological observations. While the morphological data are sound, the inference about differentiation status is not directly demonstrated and represents a hypothesis based on intermediate morphological characteristics. The comparison to previous reports (C29) provides some support but does not definitively establish the differentiation state.

results.result: The vast majority of haptomonads were non-dividing (1N1F), but a small number of dividing forms (1N2F or 2N2F) were identified. In dividing cells with long new flagella, both flagella were attached, while in cells with short new flagella only the old flagellum was attached. Four abnormal cells with multiple nuclei but single flagella were also observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C34 are supported by quantitative analysis of over 1000 cells from SBFSEM data. The observations are clearly documented with specific counts and are consistent with previous reports (C30 cites Gossage et al., 2003). The identification of dividing forms contradicts earlier suggestions that haptomonads are non-replicative, which is appropriately noted.

results.result: A small number of haptomonads (6 in ~1000 cells) showed partial or complete detachment from the stomodeal valve, potentially representing cells differentiating back to free-swimming forms. Detachment of the cuticular lining from epithelial cells was observed where many haptomonads were adhered.
results.evaluation: Claim C35 is supported by quantitative data, but C36 acknowledges alternative explanations (fixation artifacts). The interpretation that detached forms represent differentiation is speculative. Claim C37 is supported by observations consistent with previous studies, though the causal relationship between haptomonad adhesion and cuticular damage is not definitively established.

results.result: Electron tomography revealed detailed 3D ultrastructure of the haptomonad flagellum. The haptomonad attached via the distal flagellar tip with an electron-dense attachment plaque. The cell body had a shorter asymmetric extension with a wider anterior tip. The flagellar pocket had a shortened neck region with flagellar expansion and numerous junctional complexes. The flagellum contained a 9+2 axoneme extending just beyond the cell body with accessory structures (radial spokes, dynein arms) but lacked the paraflagellar rod (PFR).
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C45 are well-supported by high-resolution electron tomography data. The structural observations are detailed and quantitative (e.g., microtubule capping structures, absence of PFR). The use of Markham rotational averaging (C43) is an established method for analyzing axonemal structures. The observations are internally consistent and provide unprecedented detail of haptomonad ultrastructure.

results.result: The attachment plaque complex consisted of discrete structural layers: outer and inner dense plaques (~10 nm each) overlaying the flagellar membrane, connected to a dense filamentous layer (~100 nm). Filaments and filament bundles extended from the FAZ to the attachment interface over ~3 μm, appearing to connect the attachment interface to the cell body. The stomodeal valve had a layered structure including a putative wax layer (~10 nm). The flagellar membrane was positioned ~10 nm from the valve surface with connecting structures spanning this gap.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C53 are supported by detailed electron tomography observations with quantitative measurements of layer thicknesses and distances. The structural organization is clearly documented in the imaging data. The identification of the wax layer (C50) is supported by comparison with literature on insect cuticle structure. The observations of connecting structures with consistent spacing provide strong evidence for specific transmembrane proteins.

results.result: The haptomonad flagellar membrane showed numerous projections and indentations. Large vesicular structures were observed throughout the flagellum, and smaller vesicles were seen near the attachment interface, with one appearing to fuse with or bud from the flagellar membrane.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 are directly supported by electron tomography observations. The vesicular structures are clearly visible in the imaging data. However, the interpretation of vesicle function (discussed in C101-C103) remains speculative.

results.result: In vitro haptomonad-like cells generated on scratched plastic substrates showed morphological and ultrastructural similarity to sand fly haptomonads. SEM and SBFSEM revealed cells with short, wide cell bodies and short flagella attached via attachment plaques. The in vitro cells had shortened flagella with 9+2 axonemes without PFR, expanded FAZ areas, and layered attachment plaque complexes similar to in vivo haptomonads. Quantitative morphological comparisons showed in vitro cells had slightly longer cell bodies but were otherwise similar in flagellum length, axoneme length, and cell body width. More dividing cells were observed in vitro than in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C66 are well-supported by comparative SBFSEM and electron tomography data from in vitro and in vivo samples. Quantitative morphological measurements (C65) with statistical analysis demonstrate similarity between the two systems. The conclusion that in vitro forms are suitable for studying haptomonad biology (C66) is a reasonable inference based on the demonstrated structural similarities, though the caveat about potential differences is appropriately noted.

results.result: Time-lapse microscopy of in vitro haptomonad-like cell adhesion identified five distinct stages occurring over 2-9 hours: (1) surface exploration with flagellum and membrane streamer release, (2) initial flagellum adhesion at any point along its length, (3) stable attachment with potential flagellum loop formation (7/10 cells), (4) flagellum shortening with membrane expansion and fusion, and (5) attachment maturation with clear attachment plaque and cell body reorientation. Throughout adhesion, the cell body became shorter and wider.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C77 are supported by time-lapse microscopy data from 8 videos showing 10 adhering cells. The five stages are clearly documented with specific observations at each stage. Quantitative data on flagellum loop formation (C73) strengthens the findings. SEM confirmation of the stages (C77) provides independent validation. The sample size is modest but adequate for this descriptive analysis.

results.result: Some adhesion attempts were unsuccessful (3/10 cells), with cells detaching and swimming away before flagellum disassembly, suggesting that the initial stages (1-3) of adhesion are reversible in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 are supported by quantitative observations from time-lapse microscopy. The inference about reversibility (C79) is reasonable based on the observed detachment events. However, the generalization is limited to in vitro conditions and the sample size is small.

results.result: Fluorescence microscopy of cells expressing tagged RSP4/6 and PFR2 showed that both signals shortened in parallel with flagellum shortening during adhesion. In mature haptomonad-like cells, only short RSP4/6 signal was consistently seen, while PFR2 signal was absent in 30% (9/30) of cells, suggesting PFR disassembly during adhesion.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 are supported by fluorescence microscopy data with quantitative analysis (n=30 cells for C81). The observations are consistent with the electron microscopy findings showing absence of PFR in haptomonads (C45). The inference about PFR disassembly (C82) is reasonable based on the loss of PFR2 signal.

results.result: In vitro purified metacyclics showed very low adhesion capacity compared to promastigotes after 24 hours.
results.evaluation: Claim C83 is supported by quantitative comparison of adhesion between promastigotes and metacyclics. The experimental design is appropriate with proper controls. However, the generalization to in vivo metacyclics requires caution as in vitro purified metacyclics may not fully represent the in vivo state.

results.result: EGTA (1-2 mM) had no effect on promastigote growth in suspension but dramatically reduced adhesion in a dose-dependent manner. In contrast, EGTA treatment of already-attached cells did not cause detachment. These results indicate that Ca2+ is critical for adhesion formation but not maintenance in Leishmania in vitro, contrasting with previous findings in T. congolense and suggesting different regulatory mechanisms for adhesion in different trypanosomatids.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C90 are well-supported by experimental data with appropriate controls and replication (n=3 independent experiments). The dose-dependent effect of EGTA on adhesion formation (C85) and lack of effect on maintenance (C88) are clearly demonstrated. The comparison with T. congolense (C86) is appropriately cited, and the inference about different regulatory mechanisms (C87) is reasonable. Statistical analysis with p-values strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: The haptomonad attachment plaque has a layered architecture with inner and outer dense plaques connecting to a dense filament layer, similar in arrangement to mammalian hemidesmosomes. However, no orthologues of hemidesmosome constituent proteins are found in the L. mexicana genome.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C93 are supported by electron tomography observations (C91) and genomic analysis (C93). The structural similarity to hemidesmosomes (C92) is an appropriate inference based on morphology, and the authors correctly note the absence of protein orthologues, justifying their use of the term 'attachment plaque' rather than 'hemidesmosome.'

results.result: Filaments in the haptomonad flagellum are 8-10 nm thick, similar to intermediate or septin filaments in other eukaryotes, and filament bundles (16-20 nm) may be formed by bundling individual filaments. However, no orthologues of intermediate filament or septin proteins are present in the Leishmania genome, suggesting Leishmania may have unique filament-forming proteins.
results.evaluation: Claim C94 is supported by measurements from electron microscopy data. However, claims C95 and C97 are speculative inferences. While the absence of known filament protein orthologues (C96) is established, the conclusion about unique filament-forming proteins requires identification and characterization of the actual proteins involved, which is not provided in this study.

results.result: Connections spanning the ~10 nm gap between the flagellar membrane and stomodeal valve surface are more likely transmembrane proteins rather than flexible substances like mucus, based on their constant spacing and absence in wider gaps.
results.evaluation: Claim C98 is a reasonable inference based on the consistent spacing (~10 nm) of the connections and their absence in wider gaps. The logic is sound, though definitive identification of these structures as transmembrane proteins would require additional biochemical or proteomic analysis.

results.result: The haptomonad flagellum has undergone dramatic remodeling, with strong attachment mediated not only by the attachment plaque but also by numerous filaments and filament bundles connecting the attachment interface to the FAZ junctional complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 are supported by the comprehensive structural observations from electron tomography. The conclusion about dramatic remodeling (C99) is justified by the documented changes in flagellar structure. The inference about the role of filaments in buttressing attachment (C100) is reasonable based on the observed structural organization.

results.result: Vesicles within the flagellum may represent mechanisms for flagellar membrane removal during disassembly. Smaller vesicles near the attachment interface may contain components for attachment plaque assembly or support exo/endocytosis for releasing factors like chitinase onto the stomodeal valve surface.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103 are speculative interpretations of the observed vesicles. While the vesicles are clearly documented (C55-C56), their function is not directly demonstrated. The analogy to desmosome assembly (C102) provides some support, but these remain hypotheses requiring experimental validation.

results.result: While most haptomonads were non-dividing, dividing forms were observed, potentially representing asymmetric differentiation divisions or proliferative divisions. In cells with long new flagella, both flagella were attached, suggesting proliferative division. In cells with short new flagella, only the old flagellum was attached, suggesting attachment structure formation is post-axonemal assembly and requires sufficient flagellum length.
results.evaluation: Claim C104 is supported by SBFSEM observations. However, claims C105-C107 involve speculative interpretations about the fate of daughter cells and the nature of the divisions. While the observations are accurate and the analogies to other kinetoplastids (C105) are appropriate, the actual fate of daughter cells and the mechanisms involved require further investigation.

results.result: Sexual recombination in Leishmania occurs in the sand fly, and the close positioning of attached haptomonads may facilitate cell fusion events.
results.evaluation: Claim C109 is established knowledge supported by multiple citations. However, claim C110 is speculative inference based on spatial organization. While the hypothesis is reasonable, no direct evidence of cell fusion events or sexual recombination at the haptomonad stage is provided in this study.

results.result: A model of Leishmania adhesion was developed combining in vivo and in vitro observations. Promastigotes explore surfaces with their flagella, and if suitable positions are found, adhesion is triggered with calcium potentially playing a role. Initial adhesion stages are reversible, but a point of no return occurs. Adhesion continues with axoneme and PFR disassembly, flagellar membrane expansion, and attachment plaque assembly. Mature cells orient orthogonally to the surface. Haptomonads can divide slowly, potentially generating attached and unattached forms. Detached cells with attachment plaques may represent early differentiation to free-swimming forms. In vitro metacyclics are not adhesion competent, and laterally attached cells may represent transitional forms.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C120 represent a comprehensive model integrating multiple observations. While many components are well-supported (e.g., C111, C115, C116 based on direct observations), several aspects are speculative (e.g., C112 about calcium's role, C117 about asymmetric division, C118 about detached cells, C120 about laterally attached cells). The model appropriately acknowledges uncertainties and caveats about in vitro vs. in vivo differences. This represents a valuable synthesis but requires further experimental validation of speculative components.

results.result: The detailed 3D organization and architecture of haptomonad attachment revealed in this study will facilitate future work on identifying proteins involved in adhesion and understanding the mechanism and role of haptomonad attachment in the Leishmania life cycle.
results.evaluation: Claim C121 is a reasonable forward-looking statement about the implications of the study. The detailed structural characterization provided does establish a foundation for future molecular and functional studies, though the actual utility will depend on subsequent research.
